name: PRP under eyes

lead: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is made by drawing a person's blood and spinning it to concentrate platelets. Clinics offer it under the eyes for thin, crepey or dark skin, promoted for wrinkles and fine lines, aiming for thicker, smoother-looking under-eye skin.

Platelets carry growth factors and cytokines, and proponents propose these support tissue repair and skin quality. Wikipedia describes PRP evidence as mixed and condition-specific. No published trial of PRP specifically for under-eye skin was found, and a registered trial in the nasojugal fold (tear trough) was withdrawn.

paras: Clinics inject it under the eyes or apply it after microneedling, usually as a series of sessions. Preparation methods vary by kit and facility, and results are judged over weeks as skin quality changes.

Adverse effects are generally low in trials. The FDA does not regulate PRP itself, and clinic use is considered off-label. In 2024 the CDC reported HIV cases linked to an unlicensed spa that reused contaminated equipment.

angle.text: Users get PRP injections under the eyes to improve thin, crepey or dark skin, drawing on clinic marketing for wrinkles and fine lines. Growth factors from your own platelets are thought to support skin repair and thickness. Eye-specific trial data is limited.

lead: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is a concentrate of plasma from a person's own blood, produced by centrifugation, that keeps platelets and the growth factors they carry [1]. Under the eyes, clinics and enthusiasts use it to improve thin, crepey, dull or darkened skin and the tired, hollow look of the tear trough, the groove between lower lid and cheek [2][3][4]. It is often paired with microneedling in what is marketed as a vampire facial [1].

Reviews of PRP in general describe mixed, condition-specific evidence [1]. A 2025 systematic review of 14 studies compared PRP and platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) for periorbital rejuvenation: PRF was linked to better skin texture, wrinkles and crepiness, PRP had stronger support for pigmentation, both had mild, transient side effects and high patient satisfaction, and the authors called for larger randomised trials [2]. A 2021 systematic review of 39 studies on dark circles listed PRP among treatments reported as effective, while noting that high-quality evidence was scarce [3].

On looksmax.org, members post about PRP and vampire facials as a skin-quality and anti-aging measure and discuss PRF biofillers for the tear trough [5][6]. Clinic treatment is the setting reviews address; the CDC has reported serious infections from an unlicensed spa [1].
infobox: Intradermal or subdermal injection, sometimes with microneedling [1]
Preparation devices need FDA clearance; clinical use is off-label [1]

paras: Blood is drawn and spun in a centrifuge to remove red cells while keeping platelets, which carry growth factors and cytokines; protocols aim to concentrate platelets to about three to five times normal levels [1]. Preparation is done with commercial kits and varies between people and facilities; categories include leukocyte-rich PRP, leukocyte-reduced PRP and leukocyte platelet-rich fibrin [1]. PRF is a related fibrin-matrix preparation that forum members describe as a natural filler [6][2].

The periorbital area is difficult to treat because lower-lid skin is very thin and shows underlying features such as vessels and bone [2][4]. Dark circles have pigmentary, structural, vascular or mixed causes, including anatomy, allergy and rubbing, medication, fatigue, age and sun exposure [3][4]. The 2021 review concluded that fillers and fat grafting suit volume-loss hollows, blepharoplasty suits excess skin, topicals and peels suit pigment, and lasers give mild to moderate benefit; PRP injection was among the reported effective treatments [3]. The 2025 PRP-versus-PRF review found no evidence that either was superior [2].

Wikipedia and dermatology reviews also describe PRP in wrinkles, blemishes and hair loss [1][7]. A meta-analysis addressed PRP in alopecia [8], and a 2025 split-face trial compared adipose stem-cell exosomes with PRP on photoaged facial skin [9].
Vampire facials combine PRP with microneedling, a practice that grew popular in the 2010s [1].

PRP is used in orthopaedics, where results vary by condition: Wikipedia notes tentative support in knee osteoarthritis and mixed findings in rotator cuff disease [1][10]. Other applications include diabetic foot ulcers, hair loss and assisted reproduction, where a 2024 Cochrane review assessed intrauterine and intraovarian use [1][11]. The World Anti-Doping Agency removed intramuscular PRP from its prohibited list in January 2011 [1].

A looksmax.org member posted about completing a first PRP session with microneedling, saying he hoped to age less, and other members reacted with surprise [5]. Another thread describes a member planning periodic vampire facials and PRF biofiller in areas including the tear trough, chin and jaw, and others responded with questions [6]. Some members describe preparing PRP themselves; clinics offer the treatment under medical supervision, and this article does not cover home preparation.

Adverse effects are generally low across trials, and one review found weak evidence of harm at rates similar to untreated people [1]. Periorbital reviews report mild, transient side effects [2]. In April 2024 the CDC reported HIV diagnoses in three women who had facials at an unlicensed Albuquerque spa, where single-use blood-contaminated equipment was reused without sterilization; about 200 other former clients and partners tested negative [1].
The FDA does not regulate PRP itself because it is exempt from the traditional pathways, so clinical use is off-label; the devices used to prepare it require clearance [1].

Eye-specific evidence is limited to reviews and small studies: the 2025 systematic review of 14 periorbital PRP and PRF studies [2] and the 2021 dark-circle treatment review of 39 studies [3]. A registered trial of PRP in the nasojugal folds (NCT03255681) was withdrawn [12]. A completed phase 2/3 study (NCT01461785, n=25) evaluated PRP in fat transfer, a related use [13]. Other controlled work includes the alopecia meta-analysis [8] and a split-face trial in photoaged skin [9].
